title: Banswara: inside Rajasthan's 'City of 100 Islands' and its tribal heritage
excerpt: About 150 km south of Udaipur, the Mahi River braids into hundreds of islets around a district rich in Bhil history, Shakti Peetha temples and monsoon waterfalls.
body:
• Banswara, about 150 km south of Udaipur in southern Rajasthan, is nicknamed the "City of 100 Islands" for the hundreds of islets scattered through the Mahi River near Chacha Kota.
  • The name comes from "bans" (bamboo), once abundant here — or from Bansia, the Bhil ruler who governed the region before Jagmal Singh crowned himself its first Maharaval.
  • Bhil tribals, known as the bowmen of Rajasthan, still make up more than half the district's population.
  • Highlights include the Mahi Bajaj Sagar Dam, the Tripura Sundari temple (a Shakti Peetha), the 11th–12th-century Arthuna temples, and Mangarh Dham — remembered as the "Jallianwala Bagh of Rajasthan."

A green Rajasthan you didn't expect

Rajasthan conjures deserts, but the state's southern tip tells a different story. Banswara district is a land of grass-covered hills, rivers, lakes, islands and monsoon waterfalls — a green, water-rich pocket that travel writers increasingly call Rajasthan's most underrated offbeat destination. It sits roughly 150 km from Udaipur, making it an easy add-on to a southern Rajasthan itinerary.

The "100 islands" are real: the Mahi River (called Mahati in the Vayu Purana) braids into hundreds of small islets, concentrated around Chacha Kota, where boating and horse riding are popular. The exact count shifts with the river's mood, but the nickname has stuck. The Tropic of Cancer passes through the district — a geographic curiosity for road-trippers.

Context & Background

Banswara's history runs deep. One account traces the name to the "bans" or bamboo forests that once covered the region; another says it derives from Bansia (or Wasna), the Bhil ruler who governed here until Jagmal Singh defeated him and crowned himself Banswara's first Maharaval. The district was once known as Lodi Kashi, a town of temples, and its fertile central and western plains grow maize, wheat, rice, cotton, soybean and gram, while the Aravallis rise along the eastern side.

The Bhil tribal community — more than half the population — anchors the region's culture. That heritage includes Mangarh Dham, where some 1,500 Bhil devotees of the saint Govind Guru were killed by British forces during the freedom struggle, earning it the title "Jallianwala Bagh of Rajasthan."

Impact & Analysis

Banswara's appeal is the density of experiences in a compact area. The Mahi Bajaj Sagar Dam is the headline attraction, dramatic when its gates open in monsoon. The Kagdi Pick Up Weir on Ratlam Road offers gardens, calm water and boating. The Tripura Sundari temple — also called Turtia Mata, believed to be a Shakti Peetha — draws devotees from across the region, especially during Navratri; its black-stone idol of the goddess, with 18 arms, rides a tiger.

For history buffs, the Arthuna temples, about 55 km away, date to the 11th and 12th centuries, with carved stone idols in padmasana and khadgasana postures. The 12th-century Paraheda Shiva temple, built under King Mandlik about 22 km from town, and the 16th-century Raj Mandir (City Palace), still owned by the royal family, round out the heritage circuit. The Mandareshwar temple, a Shiva shrine inside a natural hill cave with panoramic views, gives pilgrims what locals describe as an Amarnath-like experience.

Monsoon is the magic window: waterfalls like Kagdi, Juha, Kadeliya, Bhuadara and Jhulla come alive, and the islands at Chacha Kota turn lush. Post-monsoon through winter offers the most comfortable sightseeing weather.

Diaspora Angle

For NRIs with Rajasthani roots, Banswara offers something the Jaipur–Udaipur circuit doesn't: a living tribal heritage and freedom-struggle history at Mangarh Dham, uncrowded temples, and landscapes that look nothing like the desert postcard. It's the kind of ancestral-region travel that turns a family trip into a story worth retelling.

What's Next

Banswara is still emerging as a destination — expect rustic charm rather than polished infrastructure. Reach it by road from Udaipur (about three hours), or via the nearest rail and air links at Udaipur. Travel during or just after the monsoon for the islands, dams and waterfalls at their best, and pair it with Udaipur for a trip that covers both royal Rajasthan and its tribal, riverine other half.
